source.title: Limits of Reliability and Scaling in Language Models

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some mathematical notation is flattened in the web text, but the scaling-law results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives theoretical cross-entropy scaling relationships and a compute-optimal balance using a spectral method, rather than reproducing the original empirical scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical scaling results under explicit spectral and model assumptions, but no empirical sweep of language-model size, tokens, or compute, and no test of small-run extrapolation. Its benchmark-saturation illustration and benchmark-token mutual-information analysis do not measure the scaling versions. Results quoted from other studies are not recorded as this paper’s results.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper with no training runs or loss measurements. It derives power-law data and capacity terms from task-mixture spectral assumptions (Theorems 8, 9, 11). It argues that the joint law is a max of the two terms, with the additive Chinchilla form holding only on a balanced frontier, and that the exponents depend on task spectra. That is a specific argument that the additive form and fixed exponents need restating, so T5 rather than T2. Its benchmark experiments do not measure scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one addition. The paper's main claims are an information-theoretic reliability ceiling R* and dependency-kernel-driven autoregressive degradation. From these the author derives a max-form scaling law limited by the scarcer of data and capacity, with an H(Y|X) floor. The additive Chinchilla law appears as a special case on the balanced frontier. The author also predicts that scaling one resource far beyond the other yields negligible returns.
record.recipe_differences: The paper offers a theoretical spectral derivation rather than the original studies’ empirical scaling measurements and fitted extrapolations.
record.method_sensitivity: The derived exponents depend on task-mixture spectral decay νT, target regularity μ̄, and architectural factor d. The boundary case μ̄ = νT + 1 yields a logarithmic correction rather than a pure power.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on a single task causes forgetting on another task that scales with sqrt(1-ρ²) of their dependency-kernel alignment (Prop. 13, theoretical).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Catastrophic forgetting after fine-tuning scales with misalignment of the tasks' dependency kernels.

fits_no_version.finding: Benchmark saturation index: writing benchmarks saturate well below perfect top scores, math benchmarks near perfect (Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-specific reliability ceilings cap LLM benchmark performance regardless of scale.

record.problems: The scaling results are theoretical and conditional on strong spectral, alignment, kernel-regime, and representational-budget assumptions; the paper reports no empirical scaling sweep to validate the loss law or its extrapolation. The authors also note that finite-sample estimation theory for the task quantities is open.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Benchmark saturation results and pairwise mutual-information plots are not measurements of the scaling versions; cited scaling estimates from other work are not this paper’s results.

untested.parts: No empirical loss measurements across orders of magnitude; holds only under kernel-regime and spectral assumptions.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
Compute-optimal N(C) and D(C) exponents and which resource grows faster are not derived or tested.
All: the factor d is speculated to depend on the depth-width ratio but is not tested.
All. The fine-tuning result (Prop. 13) concerns forgetting, not the scaling-law form.
No empirical comparison of fitting choices, schedules, or parameter counting.

missing.what: Regime μ̄ > νT+1: the effective data exponent saturates at β_eff=1 regardless of (μ̄−1)/νT, so the derived exponent formula fails there (theoretical; authors call it not empirically relevant).
missing.locator: Appendix B.8, Step 5, Case μ̄ > νT + 1

record.verdict_notes: No empirical scaling evidence. Cited exponent estimates (Kaplan β≈0.095, Hoffmann β≈0.34, Besiroglu α≈0.348, β≈0.366) come from other work and are used only for consistency checks. Verdicts on V1 and V7 rest on derivations under strong assumptions (kernel regime, shared eigenbasis), so they should be weighted as theoretical arguments, not observations.

versions.untested_parts: No empirical validation across several orders of magnitude; no tested model runs or empirical comparison of parameter-, token-, and compute-scaling curves.
No prediction from fitted small runs is compared with larger runs.
Does not derive parameter-count and token-count growth as explicit powers of total compute, or test which resource grows faster along a compute budget.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law form in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No test of whether downstream task performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
Does not vary empirical fitting procedures or directly compare fitted exponents across data, schedules, or parameter-counting choices; its setup dependence is derived theoretically.

rows.subject: autoregressive model
rows.operation_detail: Combines the data and capacity terms into a joint loss law with an irreducible conditional-entropy floor.

conditions.value: Assumptions of Theorems 8 and 9, including power-law spectrum, target regularity, kernel regime, and representational-budget model
Loss reducible term is determined by the scarcer of data and capacity

rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss as a function of parameters N and training tokens D
rows.value: L(N,D) = max(A/N^α, B/D^β) + H(Y|X) + o(max(N^-α, D^-β))
rows.note: The derived joint law has a max form, rather than an additive law away from the balanced frontier, and is conditional on the stated assumptions.
rows.check: Should not be 'partial' for V1. The max form is exactly a power law in the scarcer resource, matching V1's 'when the others are not the bottleneck'. The departure from the additive form bears on V7.

rows.subject: autoregressive model
rows.operation_detail: Derives the loss along a frontier where the parameter and data contributions are balanced.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss and balance between parameter and data contributions
rows.value: On the balanced frontier, L(N,D) = A/N^α + B/D^β + H(Y|X) + o(max(N^-α, D^-β)); the paper states that the strategy balances N and D.
rows.locator: Corollary 12 and discussion following Theorem 11, Section 5.1.4
rows.note: The paper gives a balance condition and loss form on that frontier, but not explicit optimal N(C) and D(C) power laws in total compute.
rows.check: Gives only a balance condition A N^-α ≍ B D^-β. It derives no N(C) or D(C) exponents. The claim that this 'justifies' Hoffmann's equal allocation would need α=β, which is not derived.

rows.subject: autoregressive model
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes the boundary case for the data exponent in the proof of Theorem 8.
rows.measure: Estimation loss versus effective data D_eff
rows.value: The loss scales as D_eff^-1 log D_eff rather than as a pure power; the paper excludes this boundary case from the theorem.
rows.locator: Appendix B.8, Theorem 8 proof, Case μ̄ = νT + 1
rows.note: A theoretical boundary case in the derivation, not an observed departure in a language-model training run.
rows.check: Theoretical boundary case, excluded from the theorem. Not an observed bend in a training curve.
